4. Various defendants by filing a joint written statement denied the material allegations and contended, inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation and that the alleged bainapatra was collusive and created. Nepal exchanged all his lands including the suit land with defendant Nos.5 and 6 and left the country forever and never came back to this country. 

 6. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding that it is barred by limitation, that the plaintiff failed to prove the genuineness of the bainapatra dated 9-2-64 and that the defendants also could not prove their cases. 

 7. The appeal preferred by the predecessor of the present petitioners as plaintiff-appellant was allowed by the lower appellate Court on the finding that the plaintiff would get the benefit of section 13 of the Limitation Act, that the suit was not barred by limitation and that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land. 

 8. The High Court Division in discharging the Rule held that the bainapatra dated 9-2-64 contains a stipulation that the vendor would execute the necessary sale deed within six months. With the expiry of 9-8-67 the suit became barred by limitation under Article 113 of the First Schedule. the plaintiff will get the benefit of section 13 of the Limitation Act as it was nowhere pleaded by the plaintiff that the vendor Nepal at any time after execution of the alleged sale deed dated 9-2-64 left the territory of Bangladesh or was absent from Bangladesh. The plaintiff had merely repeatedly stated in the plaint that the plaintiff had gone "স্থানান্তরে", which means moving from one place to another within the country. The plaintiff’s son as PW 1 also did not state in his evidence that Nepal was at any time outside of the territory of Bangladesh. The suit was therefore barred by limitation. The High Court Division also found that the bainapatra Ext.6 was found to be a genuine one by the lower appellate Court on the basis of the solitary evidence of PW 2 who is the full brother of the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not examine himself and the trial Court considering the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 came to a positive finding that the plaintiff failed to prove his bainapatra by cogent evidence. The finding of the lower appellate Court on the genuineness of the bainapatra is not binding on the revisional Court because of the non-consideration of the material evidence of PWs. 1 and 3 and also because of non-examination by the plaintiff of one Joynal Miah who is indisputably alive and was one of the four attesting witnesses to the bainapatra. 

 9. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that the circumstances of the case do not involve the application of Article 113 of the First Schedule and therefore the High Court Division erred in holding that the suit was barred by limitation. Also, he argued, that the finding as to the genuineness of Ext.6 the bainapatra was wrongly interfered with in revision by the High Court Division upon a fresh assessment of evidence. 

 10. We find that the High Court Division upon giving cogent reasons found that the plaintiff was not entitled to the benefit of section 13 of the Limitation Act as the pleading in the plaint did not attract the application of the said section. Also we find that the High Court Division in revision rightly interfered with the finding of fact of the lower appellate Court with regard to the genuieneness of the bainapatra Ext.6.
